'''''Dioscorea polystachya''''' or '''Chinese yam''' (''shānyào,'' {{lang-zh|s=山药|t=山藥}}), also called '''cinnamon-vine''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 17 December 2017}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the [[Dioscoreaceae|yam family]]. It is sometimes called '''Chinese potato''' or by its Korean name '''''ma'''''.{{r|wep}}<ref name=GRIN/> It is also called '''huaishan''' in Mandarin and '''wàaih sāan''' in [[Cantonese]].

It is a perennial climbing [[vine (botany)|vine]], native to East Asia.{{r|wep}}{{r|iccw}} The edible [[tuber]]s  are cultivated largely in East Asia and sometimes used in [[alternative medicine]]. This species of yam is unique as the tubers can be eaten raw.<ref name=fna>{{eFloras|1 |family=Dioscoreaceae |first=Lauren |last=Raz}}</ref><ref>{{eFloras|2 |family=Dioscoreaceae |first1=Chih-chi |last1=Ting |first2=Michael G. |last2=Gilbert}}</ref>

== Range ==
This plant grows throughout [[East Asia]].<ref name=":1">{{EOL |access-date = 2016-02-01}}</ref> It is believed to have been introduced to Japan in the 17th century or earlier.<ref name="tsuyuzaki">{{cite web|title=Dioscorea polystachya Turczaninow|url=http://hosho.ees.hokudai.ac.jp/~tsuyu/top/plt/yam/dioscorea/pol.html|website=(TSUYUZAKI Shiro|last=Tsuyuzaki|first=Shiro 露崎四朗|publisher=Hokkaido University|access-date=1 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528201125/http://hosho.ees.hokudai.ac.jp/~tsuyu/top/plt/yam/dioscorea/pol.html|archive-date=28 May 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> Introduced to the [[United States]] as early as the 19th century for culinary and cultural uses, it is now considered an invasive plant species.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|title = Forest Invasive Plants of the Northeastern Area - Chinese Yam or Cinnamon Vine|url = http://na.fs.fed.us/spfo/invasiveplants/factsheets/chineseyam/chineseyam.htm|website = na.fs.fed.us|access-date = 2016-02-01}}</ref><ref name=i>[https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.html?sub=4527 Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States, entry for ''Dioscorea polystachya'']</ref><ref name=feis>{{FEIS |last=Gucker |first=Corey L. |date=2009 |type=vine |genus=Dioscorea}}</ref> The plant was introduced to [[Europe]] in the 19th century during the [[European Potato Failure]], where cultivation continues to this day for the contemporary East Asian food market.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Chinese Yam (Dioscorea Opposita)|url = https://www.onlyfoods.net/chinese-yam-dioscorea-opposita.html|website = www.onlyfoods.net| date=23 May 2012 |access-date = 2016-02-01}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
{{see also|Dioscorea oppositifolia}}
The [[botanical name]]s ''Dioscorea opposita'' and ''[[Dioscorea oppositifolia]]'' have been consistently misapplied to Chinese yam.<ref name=GRIN/><ref name="fna" /><ref name="feis" /> The name ''D. opposita'' is now an accepted [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] of ''D. oppositifolia''.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |url=http://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=240599 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200313191711/https://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=240599 |url-status=dead |archive-date=March 13, 2020 |title=''Chinese yam'' |work=[[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]] (WCSP) |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] }}</ref>  Botanical works that point out the error may list, e.g., ''Dioscorea opposita'' [[Auctorum|auct.]] as a synonym of ''D. polystachya''.<ref name=GRIN/> Furthermore, neither ''D. oppositifolia'' nor the prior ''D. opposita'' have been found growing in North America and have no historical range in China or East Asia, since this grouping is exclusively native only to the [[Indian subcontinent|subcontinent of India]] and should not be confused with ''Dioscorea polystachya''.<ref name="fna" />

==Description==
[[File:Dioscorea polystachya UGA2307129.jpg|thumb|left|upright|''Dioscorea polystachya'', Chinese yam]]
''Dioscorea polystachya'' vines typically grow {{convert|3|–|5|m|sp=us}} long, and can be longer. They twine anticlockwise. The leaves are up to {{convert|11|cm|sp=us}} long and wide. They are lobed at the base and larger ones may have lobed edges. The arrangement is variable; they may be alternately or oppositely arranged or borne in whorls.

In the leaf axils appear warty rounded [[bulbil]]s under {{convert|2|cm|sp=us}} long. The bulbils are sometimes informally referred to as "yam berries" or "yamberries".<ref>{{citation
|editor-first=Thomas |editor-last=Christopher
|publisher=Timber Press |year=2011
|isbn=978-1604691863
|title=The New American Landscape: Leading Voices on the Future of Sustainable Gardening
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=x45tE8p-dqsC
|page=121
}}</ref><ref name=Toensmeier2013>{{citation
|first1=Eric |last1=Toensmeier|first2= Jonathan |last2=Bates
|publisher=Chelsea Green Publishing |year=2013
|isbn=978-1603583992
|title=Paradise Lot: Two Plant Geeks, One-Tenth of an Acre, and the Making of an Edible Garden Oasis in the City
|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=ipA1e_EXJHoC&pg=PA187
|pages=185–188
}}</ref>

New plants sprout from the bulbils or parts of them.

The flowers of Chinese yam are [[cinnamon]]-scented.

The plant produces one or more spindle-shaped<ref name=fna/> or cylindrical<ref name=feis/> tubers. The largest may weigh {{convert|10|lb}} and grow {{convert|1|m|sp=us|spell=in}} underground.<ref name=feis/> ''Dioscorea polystachya'' is more tolerant to frost and cooler climates than other yams, which is attributed to its successful introductions and establishment on many continents.

== Common names ==
[[File:Dioscorea polystachya UGA5421977.jpg|thumb|upright|In addition to larger underground tubers, Chinese yam also produces small bulbils (aerial tubers), formed where leaves join the stem. These are also edible but are described as having a bland or unappealing taste. Some compare their taste to that of new potatoes.<ref name=Toensmeier2013/>]]
In Chinese it is known as ''shānyào'' ({{lang-zh|s=山药|t=[[wikt:山藥|山藥]]|l=mountain medicine}}), ''huáishān'' ({{lang-zh|s=怀山|t=懷山|labels=no}} or  {{lang-zh|c=淮山|labels=no}}),<ref>Originated from Jiaozuo (焦作), previously known as "Huai Qing Fu (怀庆俯)" {{cite web|url = http://www.shanyao.com/a-22995-1/|title = 四大怀药的历史文化渊源|access-date = 2016-02-01|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160203061202/http://www.shanyao.com/a-22995-1/|archive-date = 2016-02-03|url-status = dead}}</ref> or ''huáishānyào'' ({{lang-zh|s=怀山药|t=懷山藥|labels=no}} or {{lang-zh|s=淮山药|t=淮山藥|labels=no|l=mountain medicine from Huai}}, i.e. the Huai Qing Fu ({{lang-zh|s=怀庆俯|t=懷慶俯|labels=no}}) region).  Rarely, it is also referred to as ''shǔyù''  ({{lang-zh|t=[[wikt:薯蕷|薯蕷]]|s=薯蓣|labels=no}}). The yam bulbils are referred to as ''shanyao dou'' ({{lang-zh|s=山药豆|t=山藥豆|l=yam bean|labels=no}}) or ''shanyao dan'' ({{lang-zh|s=山药蛋|t=山藥蛋|l=yam eggs|labels=no}}).

In Japan, three groups of this species in cultivation are recognized. The common long, cylindrical type is known as {{nihongo||[[wikt:長芋|長芋]]|nagaimo|{{lit|long yam}}}}. The {{nihongo|''ichōimo''|銀杏芋|extra='[[ginkgo]]-leaf yam'}} bears a flat, {{linktext|palmate}} shape, and the {{nihongo|''tsukune imo''|つくね芋|extra2='meatball yam'}} is round or {{linktext|globular}}.{{r|thompson}}{{sfnp|Babil|2013|p=101}} The term {{nihongo|''yamatoimo''|[[wikt:大和芋|大和芋]]|extra='Yamato [Province] yam'}} is used particularly in the [[Kantō]] region for the ''ichōimo'' in the market,<ref name=takahashi_nobuyuki/> but this is confusing since traditionally ''yamatoimo'' has also referred to ''tsukuneimo'', especially if produced in  [[Yamato Province]] (now [[Nara Prefecture]]).<ref name=miyaoi&kawana/> Cultivars of this species (such as ''yamatoimo'') is sometimes called "Japanese mountain yam",<ref name=satomi/> though that term should properly be reserved for the native ''[[Dioscorea japonica]]''.<ref name="tsuyuzaki" />

In Korea it is called ''ma'' ({{Korean|마}}), ''sanu'' ({{Korean|hangul=산우|hanja=山芋}}), ''seoyeo'' ({{Korean|hangul=서여|hanja=薯蕷|labels=no}}), or ''sanyak'' ({{Korean|hangul=산약|hanja=山藥|labels=no}}).

In Sri Lanka in Sinhala it is called ''wal ala'' ({{lang|si|වැල් අල}}). It is sometimes called Korean yam.

In Vietnam, the yam is called ''củ mài'' or ''khoai mài''. When this yam is processed to become a medicine, the yam is called ''hoài sơn'' or ''tỳ giải''.

In the [[Ilokano language|Ilocano]] of the northern Philippines it is called ''tuge''.

In [[Latin American]] countries it is known as camote del cerro or white ñame. 

In [[Manipuri (Meiteilon Language)|Manipuri]] it is called as "Ha".

== In alternative medicine ==
Creams and dietary supplements made from the related ''[[Dioscorea villosa]]'' are claimed to contain human hormones and promoted as a medicine for a variety of purposes, including [[cancer prevention]] and the treatment of [[Crohn's disease]] and [[whooping cough]]. However, according to the [[American Cancer Society]], the claims are false and there is no evidence to support these substances being either safe or effective.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.cancer.org/treatment/treatmentsandsideeffects/complementaryandalternativemedicine/herbsvitaminsandminerals/wild-yam|title = Wild Yam|date = November 2008|publisher = [[American Cancer Society]]|access-date = 21 September 2013|archive-date = 2 May 2015|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150502110422/http://www.cancer.org/treatment/treatmentsandsideeffects/complementaryandalternativemedicine/herbsvitaminsandminerals/wild-yam|url-status = dead}}</ref> Huáishān has also been used in traditional Chinese medicine.<ref>Xu, Dermatology in Traditional Chinese Medicine, 2004</ref>

==As an invasive species==
''Dioscorea polystachya'' was introduced to the United States in the 1800s when it was planted as an [[ornamental plant|ornamental]] or food crop. It and other introduced yam species now grow wild there. It is troublesome in [[Great Smoky Mountains National Park]], where its range is "rapidly expanding", particularly into the Tennessee Valley where different native, hybrid and/or invasive non-native variants of [[morning glory]] and [[bindweed]] as well as invasive kudzu and [[cuscuta]] (dodder) have all become problematic and are similar in appearance to the fast-moving and often mishandled tubers. 

As Chinese yam and air potatoes continue to destroy entire swaths of gardens and yards though are not yet classified as invasive in these areas, residents seeking to eat the tuber plant their vines in unprotected land while residents seeking removal chop the tops off of vines at ground level and compost or mulch them before realizing this only makes the problem worse and that no weed killers on the market are able to rid a garden or yard of the plant. The newest solution from Florida for people in Florida and surrounding states experiencing harm to their property and wishing a reprieve from these plant pests is to request free Air Potato Beetles. However, the beetles continue to elude Tennesseans due to various government regulations and the lack of others. <ref name=feis/> It is most prevalent in moist habitat types. It is more tolerant of frost than other yams and can occur in temperate climates as far north as [[New York (state)|New York]].<ref name=feis/><ref>{{BONAP|ref |genus=Dioscorea |species=polystachya}}</ref>

==Culinary uses==
[[Image:Tororo (grated Dioscorea opposita).jpg|thumb|Grated ''Dioscorea polystachya'' (Japanese ''[[Tororo (food)|tororo]]'')]]
The tubers of ''D. polystachya'' can be eaten raw (grated or sliced<ref name=andoh-washoku/>), while most other yams must be cooked before consumption (due to harmful substances in the raw state).<ref name=thompson/>

First the skin needs to be removed by peeling (or by scraping off using a hard-bristled brush).<ref name=andoh-kansha/><ref name=watanabe_maki/> This may cause a slight irritation to the hand, and wearing a latex glove is advised, but if an itch develops then lemon juice or vinegar may be applied.<ref name=watanabe_maki/><ref name=andoh-washoku/>

The peeled whole [[tuber]]s are briefly soaked in a vinegar-water solution, to neutralize irritant [[oxalate]] crystals found in their skin,<ref name=thompson/> and to prevent discoloration.<ref name=andoh-kansha/> The raw vegetable is starchy and bland, [[mucilaginous]]<!--slippery--> when cut or grated,{{r|fpc}}<ref name=andoh-washoku/> and may be eaten plain as a side dish, or added to noodles, etc.
===East Asian cuisine===
==== Chinese cuisine ====
{{Unreferenced section|date=December 2021}}
Chinese yam is referred to as ''shānyào'' ({{lang-zh|s=山药|t=山藥|labels=no}}), or mountain medicine, in Chinese traditional medicine, or referred to as huáishān (怀山; 懷山 or 淮山) in the culinary usage. The tuber is consumed raw, steamed, or [[Deep frying|deep-fried]]. It is added to savory soups, or can be sweetened with a berry sauce. When used fresh, the tuber is peeled before slicing and using them in stir-fries (mainly in Cantonese cuisine). Oftentimes, Chinese yam can be found sold in prepared, dried slices in dried goods specialty shops. When using the dry ingredient in soups, the slices need to be soaked before adding them to soups to cook.

==== Japanese cuisine ====
[[Image:Mugitoro gohan 2.jpg|thumb|left|Mugitoro gohan]]
In Japanese cuisine, both the Chinese yam cultivars and the [[Japanese yam]] (often wild-foraged) are used interchangeably in dishes. The difference is that ''nagaimo'' tends to be more watery, while the native Japanese yam is more viscous.<ref name=japantimes-15-07-15/>

[[Tororo (food)|Tororo]] is the mucilaginous [[purée]] made by grating varieties of the Chinese yam (''nagaimo'', ''ichōimo'', ''tsukuneimo'')<ref name=thompson/> or the native Japanese yam.<ref name=ocf /> The classic Japanese culinary technique is to grate the yam by grinding it against the rough grooved surface of a ''[[suribachi]]'', an earthenware [[mortar and pestle|mortar]].{{sfnp|Andoh|2012b|p=276}} Or the yam is first grated crudely using an ''[[oroshigane]]'' grater, and subsequently worked into a smoother paste in the ''suribachi'' using a wooden pestle.{{r|theeast}}

The ''tororo'' is mixed with other ingredients that typically include ''tsuyu'' broth ([[soy sauce]] and [[dashi]]), sometimes [[wasabi]] or [[Scallion|green onions]],<ref name=nrhs/><ref name=hara_luiz/> and eaten over rice or {{illm|mugimeshi{{!}}''mugimeshi''|ja|麦飯}} (steam-cooked blend of rice and [[barley]]).<ref name=thompson/><ref name=belleme/><ref name=japantimes-15-07-15/>

The tororo poured over [[Sashimi|raw tuna]] (''[[maguro]]'') sliced into cubes is called ''yamakake'', and eaten with soy sauce and [[wasabi]].<ref name=nrhs/>

The ''tororo'' may also be  poured over noodles to make ''tororo [[udon]]/[[soba]]''.<ref name=japantimes-15-07-15/> Noodles with grated yam over it is also called ''yamakake''.<ref name=andoh-kansha/>

Grated yam is also used as a [[Binder (material)|binding agent]] in the batter of ''[[okonomiyaki]]''.<ref name=japantimes-15-07-15/>

Sometimes the grated yam is used as an <!--leavening and whitening-->additive for making the skin of the [[manjū]] confection, in which case the product is called {{nihongo|{{ill|jōyo manjū|ja|薯蕷饅頭}}|薯蕷饅頭||"yam manjū"}}.<ref name=sasaki/><ref name=rheology/> The yam is also used in making a regional confection called ''[[karukan]]'', a specialty of the [[Kyūshū]] region.<ref name=japantimes-15-07-15/>

==== Korean cuisine ====
In [[Korean cuisine|Korea]], there are two main types of Chinese yam; the straight, tube-shaped variant is called ''jangma'' ({{Korean|장마|lit="long ''ma''"}}), while ''danma'' ({{Korean|단마|lit="short ''ma''"}}) refers to the variant, which grows shorter, cluster-like tubes.<ref>{{cite web|last = 지식백과|first = Naver|url = https://terms.naver.com/entry.nhn?cid=42776&docId=4368451&categoryId=59916|title = 마|access-date = 11 June 2019}}</ref> Both are used in cooking and the tubers are prepared in a variety of ways. They are most commonly consumed raw, after the skinned roots have been blended with water, milk or yogurt (occasionally with additional honey) to create a nourishing drink known as ''majeup'' ({{lang|ko|마즙}}) or "''ma'' juice" ({{lang|ko|마주스}}). Alternatively, the peeled tubers are cut into pieces and served—either raw, after cooking, steaming or frying, along with seasoning sauces.

== Cultivation ==
[[File:Kagamaruimo.jpg|thumb|''Kaga-maruimo'', a Japanese cultivar]]
The Chinese yam's growing cycle spans approximately one year, and should be planted between winter and spring. The traditional methods growing it are: using smaller tubers, top cut of bigger tubers or through cuttings of branches. The first two methods can produce 20 cm (7.8 in) long tubers and above. The latter produces smaller tubers (10 cm or 4 in) that are usually replanted for the next year.

Between 7 and 9 months of replanting Chinese yam tubers, their leaves start to get dry (a common fact in plants that grow tubers), which indicates that the tubers are ready for harvest. In home gardens generally only what will be consumed is harvested, with the rest left in the pot in moist soil.<ref>{{cite web|last = Takeguma|first = Massahiro|url = http://cultivozen.massahiro.com/2013/07/o-cultivo-do-inhame-tororo-growing.html?lang=en|title = Growing Nagaimo|access-date = 26 July 2013}}</ref>
The tuber is not frost-hardy.
